title: Which setups fit which style
teaches: Every setup runs on a clock: intraday tools like VWAP, floor pivots and opening-gap fades for the day trade, daily-chart setups like flags for the swing, weekly bases above a rising 30-week average for the position hold; the entry can be timed on a shorter chart, but the stop, the target and the exit follow the setup's own chart.

facts.quote: Day traders rapidly buy and sell stocks throughout the day in the hope that their stocks will continue climbing or falling in value for the seconds to minutes they own the stock
facts.claim: A day trader owns a stock for seconds to minutes, inside one session.

facts.quote: True day traders do not own any stocks overnight because of the extreme risk that prices will change radically from one day to the next, leading to large losses.
facts.claim: A true day trader is flat by the close, because prices can change sharply overnight.

facts.claim: New day traders usually lose heavily at first, and many never become profitable.

facts.claim: Trading through the day takes a lot of time and constant attention.

facts.claim: Intraday traders go after small moves, usually in volatile stocks.

facts.quote: Frequent trading can also come with higher costs that might erode your returns
facts.claim: More trading means more costs eating into returns.

facts.quote: Day traders are likely to pursue an aggressive style with high activity levels. The goals would be focused on quick trades, small profits, and very tight stop-loss levels.
facts.claim: Day traders aim for quick trades and small gains, with very tight stops.

facts.claim: Day traders work off intraday charts, and it takes a lot of focus.

walkthroughs.title: Three clocks, three charts
steps: A day trader is in and out the same day, holding for seconds to hours. The work happens on intraday charts.
A swing trader holds for days or weeks. The setup usually lives on the daily chart, often timed on an hourly one.
A position trader rides a trend for weeks or months. Many work off the weekly chart.
Pick setups that run on the clock you can actually keep.

walkthroughs.title: One shape, any chart
steps: A breakout from a sideways range shows up on a 1-minute chart and on a weekly chart.
Bulkowski runs one on the 5-minute chart with a tight stop. Weinstein's method buys a weekly base breakout and holds for months.
Stops scale too. Tight on the 5-minute chart. Bulkowski's Weinstein rules skip a trade if the first stop is over 20% away.
Size from the stop. The wider the stop, the smaller the position.

walkthroughs.title: Entry chart, holding clock
steps: Use three charts. The longer sets the trend, your main one gives the signal, a shorter one times the entry.
Our Kicker is a daily setup. One entry is the day-one break of the 30-minute opening range.
The trail is each higher low or the 10-day average. The intraday entry doesn't make it a day trade.

questions.q: You'll be in and out the same day, every trade. Which chart do you trade off?
choices: A 5- or 15-minute intraday chart
The daily chart, one bar a day
The weekly chart, a bar a week
Whichever chart looks cleanest
questions.why: A 5- or 15-minute intraday chart. A day trade opens and closes in the same session, held for seconds, minutes or hours. Day traders use intraday charts for timely entries and exits. Investopedia's day trader trades off the 15-minute chart and reads the short-term trend on the 5-minute. A daily or weekly bar would hold the whole trade inside one bar. Longer charts still have a job: a 60-minute chart can set the day trader's trend.
questions.lesson_line: Your holding time picks the chart. Trades that last minutes need minute bars.

wrong.The daily chart, one bar a day: One bar per day. Your whole trade would sit inside a single bar, entry and stop and all.
wrong.The weekly chart, a bar a week: That's for trends that run weeks or months. Your trade is over long before one bar closes.
wrong.Whichever chart looks cleanest: Your holding time picks the chart, not the picture. A clean daily or weekly setup can't time a trade that lasts minutes.

questions.simple: A 5- or 15-minute chart, because a trade that lasts minutes to hours needs bars that short.

questions.q: VWAP, the volume-weighted average price, carries over from one day to the next, like a 20-day moving average does.
questions.why: False. VWAP is built from one session's intraday data, from the open to the close. At the next open a new calculation starts, unrelated to the day before. The 20-day average in the question spans many sessions, and VWAP spans one. That makes VWAP a one-day reference, best suited to intraday work.
questions.lesson_line: VWAP lives inside one session. That makes it an intraday line.
questions.simple: False, because VWAP starts over at every open, so it never carries from one day to the next.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Bulkowski's opening gap-down setup, in off the 5-minute chart and out off the 1- or 2-minute, is a ___ trading setup.
questions.why: Day. Bulkowski calls this opening-gap setup a day trading setup. He enters off the 5-minute chart and times the exit on the 1- or 2-minute. Investopedia lists fading the gap among day traders' techniques. A gap alone does not make a day trade: ChartSchool applies its gap strategies to daily and weekly gaps too. A short exit chart alone does not either, since a swing trade can time its exit on a shorter chart.
questions.lesson_line: The setup's own plan sets the clock. Bulkowski built this gap trade to finish inside the session.
questions.simple: Day, because Bulkowski built this gap setup as a day trade, in and out off minute charts.

reasons: the key rests on Bulkowski's own label (f52); the Bulkowski sourcing decision is still open
fixed in wave9 (the exit-chart rule that contradicted q17 and w3 is gone)

questions.q: A stock clears a long base on the weekly chart, above a rising 30-week average. Who is this setup built for?
choices: A trader holding for months
A day trader, flat by the close
A swing trader holding 1 to 5 days
An investor holding for decades
questions.why: A trader holding for months. Weinstein's stages are read on the weekly chart, with a 30-week moving average for timing. Bulkowski puts a trader's hold with this method at 2 to 4 months, and an investor's at up to a year. Schwab says position traders hold for weeks or months. One weekly bar alone runs Monday's open to Friday's close.
questions.lesson_line: A weekly setup runs on a weekly clock. Plan for months, not days.

wrong.A day trader, flat by the close: A weekly bar takes five sessions to form. A day trader is long gone before one closes.
wrong.A swing trader holding 1 to 5 days: One to five days fits inside a single weekly bar. A setup built on a 30-week average needs more time than that.
wrong.An investor holding for decades: Even an investor using this method holds up to about a year, in Bulkowski's reading. The weekly stages time the trade. It is not buy and forget.

questions.simple: A trader holding for months, because a setup built on weekly bars takes months to play out.

reasons: hold lengths differ by source; the key uses only the order of styles (conflicts)

questions.q: A breakout from a sideways range can be traded on a 1-minute chart or on a weekly chart.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski says his breakout setup can be used on any time scale. He runs it on the 1- or 5-minute chart with a tight stop. Weinstein's method buys a breakout above a base read on the weekly chart. ChartSchool says the same of gaps: its strategies apply to intraday, daily and weekly gaps. The shape is the same on both. What changes is the chart you read it on.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern doesn't pick your style. The chart you read it on does.
questions.simple: True, because the same breakout shape can be traded on any time scale, from 1-minute bars to weekly ones.

reasons: for range breakouts the key rests on Bulkowski alone (f51); ChartSchool says it of gaps (conflicts)
fixed before (why hedged to 'can be used')

questions.q: The shortest chart is the most reliable, because it has the newest data.
questions.why: False. As a general rule, the longer the time frame, the more reliable the signals. Drill down and the charts fill up with false moves and noise. Short charts do show more detail, but detail is not reliability. It is a general rule, not a law. A short chart still has a job: timing the entry and exit.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a trade on the chart it was built on, not on a noisier one.
questions.simple: False, because short charts carry more false moves and noise, so longer charts usually give better signals.

reasons: fixed before (why names it a general rule)

questions.q: Our Launchpad trails under the rising 21-day average. Which chart do you manage that trade on?
choices: The daily chart
The 5-minute chart
The weekly chart
The hourly chart
questions.why: The daily chart. Our Launchpad trails under the rising 21-day average, or under each higher low. A 21-day average is built from daily bars, one bar per day. Our default trail sells on a close below the 10-day or 21-day average. So the trail and the higher lows both live on the daily chart. A shorter chart can still time the entry, but it does not change where the trade is managed.
questions.lesson_line: Read the trail to find the clock. A daily average means a daily-chart trade.

wrong.The 5-minute chart: A 21-day average gets one new bar a day. Five-minute bars add noise the plan doesn't trade on.
wrong.The weekly chart: Too slow. One weekly bar runs Monday to Friday and hides the daily higher lows the trail steps up under.
wrong.The hourly chart: An hourly chart can time a swing entry. But a 21-period line there spans 21 hours, not 21 days, so it is a different trail.

questions.simple: The daily chart, because a 21-day average is built from daily bars, so the trail lives there.

reasons: rests on our trade plan (TRADE_PLANS.md, Launchpad row)

questions.story: You have the whole session free to watch the screen. Holding through overnight news keeps you up at night.
questions.q: Which setups fit you best?
choices: 5-minute setups, flat by the close
Daily flags held for a few weeks
Weekly breakouts held for months
Daily flags, tight overnight stop
questions.why: 5-minute setups, flat by the close. True day traders own nothing overnight, because prices can change sharply from one day to the next. Day trading needs continuous attention, and you have the whole session free. A tight stop would not fix a swing trade for you, because a gap can jump the stop. Know the costs too: frequent trading can bring higher costs that eat into returns.
questions.lesson_line: Your hours and your nerves pick the clock. The clock picks the setups.

wrong.Weekly breakouts held for months: Months of nights and weekends, each with that same gap risk. The opposite of what you want.
wrong.Daily flags held for a few weeks: Swing trades sit through the night, and news while the market is shut can gap the open. That's the risk that keeps you up.
wrong.Daily flags, tight overnight stop: A stop can't cap a gap. News while the market is shut can open the stock past your stop, so the overnight risk stays.

questions.simple: 5-minute setups, flat by the close, because you can watch all day and then hold nothing overnight.

questions.q: Yesterday's high was $56, the low $48 and the close $55. What's today's base pivot point for your 5-minute chart?
questions.why: The base pivot is the simple average of the prior high, low and close. 56 + 48 + 55 = 159. 159 / 3 = 53. For 1- to 15-minute charts, ChartSchool takes those from the prior day. Once set, the pivots stay fixed all day. Tomorrow's pivot comes from today's bar.
questions.lesson_line: Intraday pivots come from yesterday's bar and last one session. They're day-trader levels.
questions.simple: $53, because the base pivot is the plain average of yesterday's high, low and close.

wrong.$55.00: Used only the close. The pivot averages the high, low and close.
wrong.$52.00: Averaged just the high and low. The close goes in too.
wrong.$159.00: Added the three prices and forgot to divide by 3.

questions.story: A stock rallies from $150 to $185 in three weeks on heavy volume. Then it drifts sideways for two weeks on lighter volume.
questions.q: Which plan fits a breakout from this flag?
choices: Swing it: hold days to weeks
Day trade it: out by the close
Buy and hold it for years
Skip it: the volume dried up
questions.answer: Swing it: hold days to weeks
questions.why: Swing it: hold days to weeks. Schwab calls a bull flag breakout a classic swing setup. ChartSchool calls flags short-term continuation patterns that ideally form over one to four weeks. A setup built over weeks of daily bars fits a hold of days to weeks. It is not a promise. The stop goes where the reason for the trade has failed.
questions.lesson_line: A flag is a short pause in a fast move. Trade it on a swing clock.

wrong.Day trade it: out by the close: The pattern formed over two weeks of daily bars. A day trade ends at the close, long before a daily setup has room to work.
wrong.Buy and hold it for years: Flags are short-term continuation patterns. Holding for years is investing, a different plan with a different exit.
wrong.Skip it: the volume dried up: Lighter volume in the pause is normal for a flag. In ChartSchool's example, volume expanded on the advance and contracted during the flag.

questions.simple: Swing it, because a flag that forms over weeks of daily bars is built for a hold of days to weeks.

reasons: Schwab and ChartSchool agree; Schwab refused WebFetch on 2026-11-12, last confirmed by the checker 2026-11-09

questions.q: Weinstein's average is 30 weeks long. A normal week has 5 trading days. About how many days does it cover on a daily chart?
questions.why: About 150 days: 30 weeks of 5 sessions each. So Weinstein's 30-week line sits close to a 150-day average on a daily chart. Close, not equal. A weekly bar closes on Friday, so the weekly average uses one close a week, and a short week has fewer sessions.
questions.lesson_line: A weekly line has a rough daily twin. Know where the long-term holders' line sits.
questions.simple: About 150 days, because 30 weeks times 5 trading days a week comes to 150.

deeper.counter: A 150-day line on your daily chart is a stand-in, not a copy. The weekly average takes one close per week, the Friday close. The daily one takes every close. A short week has fewer sessions than a normal one. So expect the two lines to sit near each other, not on top of each other.

choices: 150 days
180 days
210 days
1,500 days

wrong.210 days: Counted every calendar day in a week. Only trading days count.
wrong.180 days: Counted six days a week. Markets are open five.
wrong.1,500 days: A decimal slip: ten times too big.

questions.story: You day trade. Stock A moves about 0.5% a day on thin volume. Stock B moves about 4% a day on heavy volume.
questions.q: Which one fits your style?
choices: Stock B, it has range and volume
Stock A, it's calmer to hold
Either one, only the setup matters
Stock B, and size up for its range
questions.answer: Stock B, it has range and volume
questions.why: Stock B. A day trader needs a stock that moves enough in a day to make a profit. Investopedia says a small daily range or light daily volume rules a stock out. FINRA notes that intraday traders go after small moves, usually in volatile stocks. A 4% daily move gives room to work. A 0.5% move on thin volume leaves little to take. The range picks the stock, not the size: we size from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Day trades need movement and liquidity. A quiet stock gives a day trader nothing to work with.

wrong.Stock A, it's calmer to hold: Calm is fine for a longer hold. A day trader needs movement inside one session, and a small daily range leaves little to take.
wrong.Either one, only the setup matters: The stock has to fit the style too. A small daily range or light volume rules a stock out for a day trader.
wrong.Stock B, and size up for its range: Stock B fits, but not the bigger size. We size from the stop, and the wider the stop, the smaller the position.

questions.simple: Stock B, because a day trader needs a stock that moves enough in one day, with plenty of volume.

questions.q: VWAP works as a trailing stop for a three-week swing trade.
questions.why: False. VWAP starts fresh at every open, unrelated to the day before. So it can't follow a trade across three weeks. A three-week swing needs a line that spans days: ChartSchool says 5- to 20-period averages suit short-term trading. Our default trail is the 10-day or the 21-day average, and we sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Trail with a line that lasts as long as the trade.
questions.simple: False, because VWAP starts over at every open, so it can't follow a trade that lasts three weeks.

reasons: ChartSchool and Schwab agree; the house trails appear only in the why

questions.q: You trade off the daily chart. Elder says multiply your timeframe by five for the bigger trend. Which chart is that?
choices: The weekly chart
The monthly chart
The hourly chart
The zoomed-out daily
questions.why: The weekly chart. Elder calls your trading chart the intermediate one and multiplies it by five for the long-term one. Five daily bars make a week. ChartSchool says traders on daily charts can move to weekly charts for the long-term trend. Investors on weekly charts can step up to monthly ones. The factor of five is Elder's recommendation, one well-known method.
questions.lesson_line: Your trend chart sits one step above your trading chart.

wrong.The monthly chart: That's the step above the weekly. Investors who work off weekly charts can use the monthly for the bigger picture.
wrong.The hourly chart: That's shorter than your chart, not longer. It can time an entry, but it can't set the bigger trend.
wrong.The zoomed-out daily: Zooming out shows more daily bars, not a longer timeframe. Elder's step multiplies the timeframe by five, which lands on the weekly.

questions.simple: The weekly chart, because five daily bars make a week, so it is one step up from the daily.

questions.story: You swing trade off the daily chart. Last month's high was $120, low $100, close $116. Yesterday's high was $118, low $112, close $115.
questions.q: By ChartSchool's rule, which base pivot fits your daily chart this month?
choices: $112, from last month's bar
$115, yesterday's bar
$116, last month's close
$110, the midpoint
questions.why: $112, from last month's bar. On ChartSchool's rule, daily charts take their pivots from the prior month's high, low and close. Here that is (120 + 100 + 116) / 3 = 112. They stay fixed for the whole month. Yesterday's bar sets the pivots for 1- to 15-minute charts, so it would reset every day. The pivot is an average, never just the close.
questions.lesson_line: Your levels scale with your chart. A day trader's pivot doesn't fit a swing trader's clock.

wrong.$115, yesterday's bar: That's yesterday's average, the pivot for 1- to 15-minute charts. It resets every day, too fast for a daily chart.
wrong.$116, last month's close: The pivot isn't the close. It's the average of the high, low and close.
wrong.$110, the midpoint: That's halfway between the high and the low. The base pivot is the average of three numbers: the high, the low and the close.

questions.simple: $112, because a daily chart's pivot comes from last month's high, low and close, not yesterday's.

reasons: the monthly-pivot rule is one publisher's convention (ChartSchool f18); other platforms let the user pick (conflicts)

questions.story: You buy a 5-minute breakout as a day trade. To give it room, you set your stop under last week's low, 8% away.
questions.q: What's the problem with that stop?
choices: It's a weekly stop on a day trade
None, more room means fewer stop-outs
It should sit under the 200-day average
It should be a mental stop instead
questions.answer: It's a weekly stop on a day trade
questions.why: It's a weekly stop on a day trade. Day traders aim for quick trades and small profits, with very tight stops. Bulkowski's 5-minute breakout uses a tight stop as price climbs. A stop goes where the reason for the trade has failed. Here that is a 5-minute level, not last week's low. An 8% stop gives back far more than a day trade's small gains can win.
questions.lesson_line: Room isn't free. Put the stop where this trade's idea fails.

wrong.None, more room means fewer stop-outs: Fewer stop-outs, but each one costs far more than a day trade's quick, small gains can win back.
wrong.It should sit under the 200-day average: That's an even longer clock. The 200-day is a long-term average, not a day trader's line.
wrong.It should be a mental stop instead: The distance is the problem, not the order type. We keep a real stop order with the broker, never one in our head.

questions.simple: The stop is far too wide for a day trade, which needs a tight stop where the 5-minute idea fails.

deeper.trap: Sizing down to fit the 8% stop seems to fix it. We do size from the stop: the wider the stop, the fewer the shares. But a day trader is flat by the close, so a stop under last week's low may never be reached. The close becomes the real exit, and the 5-minute idea has no stop at all. Fix the stop first: put it where the 5-minute breakout fails, then size from it.

reasons: ChartSchool, Bulkowski and Schwab agree; stable

questions.story: You buy our Kicker on the day-one 30-minute opening-range break. At 3:55 p.m. it's up, short of 3R, and well above your stop.
questions.q: What does the plan say to do?
choices: Hold it; trail on the daily chart
Sell it, it was an intraday entry
Sell half of it before the close
Hold it; trail on the 30-minute chart
questions.answer: Hold it; trail on the daily chart
questions.why: Hold it, and trail on the daily chart. The day-one 30-minute break was only the entry. The Kicker trails under each higher low or under the 10-day average, and we sell on a close below it. We swing trade: days to a few weeks. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. Nothing in the plan sells at the close. The stop stays with the broker overnight as a real order.
questions.lesson_line: The entry chart times the buy. The trail sets the clock.

wrong.Sell it, it was an intraday entry: The entry chart doesn't set the clock. Swing traders often take a daily setup and time the entry on a shorter chart.
wrong.Sell half of it before the close: He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy. Nothing in the plan sells at the close.
wrong.Hold it; trail on the 30-minute chart: The 30-minute bar only timed the buy. Our Kicker trails under each higher low or the 10-day average, a daily-chart trail.

questions.simple: Hold it, because the 30-minute break only timed the buy, and the plan trails the trade on the daily chart.

deeper.trap: Holding overnight means news can gap the stock below your stop at the open. Our rule for that: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. And if those first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51) and the Kicker plan

questions.q: Day trading is the safe style, since you never hold anything overnight.
questions.why: False. Being flat overnight removes overnight gap risk, not all risk. The SEC says day traders typically suffer severe financial losses in their first months, and many never turn a profit. FINRA adds that frequent trading brings higher costs that can eat into returns. Day trading swaps one risk for others. It is not the safe style.
questions.lesson_line: Flat overnight is not the same as safe.
questions.simple: False, because being flat at night only removes gap risk, and new day traders often lose heavily anyway.

deeper.trap: Flat overnight sounds safe, because nothing can gap against you while you sleep. But a day trader takes many more trades, each with its own costs, and must watch all session. The SEC says day traders typically lose heavily in their first months. Less time at risk per trade is not less risk in total.

reasons: SEC and FINRA (Tier 1); the SEC page is dated but only its timeless lines are used

questions.story: You take a day trade off the 5-minute chart. Your target is the stock's high from three months ago, 15% above your entry.
questions.q: How does that target fit the trade?
choices: Too far for a one-day clock
Fine, a big target is a bonus
Fine, hold overnight until it hits
Irrelevant, only the stop counts
questions.answer: Too far for a one-day clock
questions.why: Too far for a one-day clock. Day traders aim for quick trades and small profits, and a day trade can run out of time before it pays. A high from three months ago is a daily-chart level, a target for a longer clock. A true day trader is flat by the close, so the 15% would have to come in one session. Pick a target one session can reach.
questions.lesson_line: Match the target to the clock. A day trade aims for what one session can give.

wrong.Fine, a big target is a bonus: A day trade aims for quick, small gains. A level from three months ago is a target for a longer clock.
wrong.Fine, hold overnight until it hits: That turns a day trade into a swing trade halfway through, with a stop built for minutes.
wrong.Irrelevant, only the stop counts: The stop caps the loss, but the target is the payoff. A day trade aims for quick, small gains and can run out of time before it pays.

questions.simple: It is too far, because a day trade aims for small gains it can reach before the close.

deeper.trap: The level isn't wrong, it is on the wrong clock. A three-month-old high is a fine target for a swing trade off the daily chart. A day trade off the 5-minute chart needs an exit inside today's session. Keep the far target and the close becomes your real exit, and the plan never said so.

questions.story: The market has chopped sideways for months. Breakouts fail within days, and no group leads for long.
questions.q: Which style has the hardest time here, and why?
choices: Position trading: no trend to ride
Day trading: too little range in a day
Day trading: breakouts fail in days
Position trading: costs pile up
questions.answer: Position trading: no trend to ride
questions.why: Position trading: no trend to ride. Position traders are trend followers, and they hold as long as the trend stays intact. Investopedia calls the style ideally suited to a bull market with a strong trend. In a flat, sideways market, it says day trading might have the advantage. Without a strong trend, moving average crossover signals also get whipsawed.
questions.lesson_line: Long holds need a trend to ride. No trend, nothing to hold for.

wrong.Day trading: too little range in a day: Nothing here says the daily range shrank. Chop takes away a lasting trend, and that hurts the longest hold the most.
wrong.Position trading: costs pile up: Right style, wrong reason. Costs pile up with frequent trading, and a position trader holds for weeks or months.
wrong.Day trading: breakouts fail in days: A day trade is out by the close, before a breakout has days to fail. In a flat, sideways market, Investopedia says day trading might even have the advantage.

questions.simple: Position trading, because it needs a lasting trend to ride, and a choppy market doesn't give one.

deeper.trap: 'Breakouts fail within days' sounds like trouble for the fastest style. But a day trade is over by the close and needs only enough movement inside one session. A position trade needs the trend to keep going for weeks or months, and a choppy market takes that away. That is why Investopedia says day trading might even have the advantage when the market goes sideways.

reasons: the ranking of styles in chop rests on one publisher (Investopedia f64, f65), which WebFetch cannot reach; Schwab and ChartSchool back the principle
choices rewritten in wave9 (the scalping near-synonym is gone)

questions.story: You can watch the first 30 minutes of the session. Then you're in meetings until the close.
questions.q: Which plan fits your day?
choices: Buy early with a stop, then hold
Scalp the 1-minute chart
Trade VWAP bounces to close
Buy, then set the stop tonight
questions.answer: Buy early with a stop, then hold
questions.why: Buy early with a stop, then hold. Make the entry in the first 30 minutes, while you can watch, with a market order. Put the stop in with the broker as a real order. We swing trade: days to a few weeks, so the trade can run without you at the screen. Scalping and VWAP trading both need your eyes on the market all session. A day trade would also need you back before the close to get flat.
questions.lesson_line: Pick an entry you can make in the time you have, then walk away.

wrong.Scalp the 1-minute chart: Scalping needs you at the screen all session. You're in meetings.
wrong.Trade VWAP bounces to close: VWAP bounces happen all session long, and you're in meetings for nearly all of it.
wrong.Buy, then set the stop tonight: The stop goes in with the entry. A stop marks where the trade has failed, and ours sits with the broker as a real order.

questions.simple: Buy early with a real stop in, then hold, because scalping and VWAP trades need you at the screen all day.

deeper.trap: A resting buy order looks like the answer for a busy trader: park it and walk away. That is not how we enter. Our entries are market orders, made while we can watch the fill, and the stop then sits with the broker. So use the 30 minutes you have: enter, set the real stop, then go to your meetings.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 market orders, D41 real stop)

questions.story: On the weekly chart, a stock sits under a falling 30-week average. Today it breaks out hard on the 5-minute chart. You want to hold it for months.
questions.q: What does the bigger chart tell you?
choices: Pass, the weekly trend says no
Buy, a breakout is a breakout
Buy, with a tight 5-minute stop
Pass, the 5-minute chart is noise
questions.answer: Pass, the weekly trend says no
questions.why: Pass: the weekly trend says no. A months-long hold rides the weekly trend. Weinstein's buy, in Bulkowski's reading, needs a close above a rising 30-week average, and here price sits under a falling one. Elder takes a daily buy only when the weekly chart shows a clear uptrend. A 5-minute breakout can time an entry, but it can't overrule the weekly chart.
questions.lesson_line: For a long hold, the weekly chart gets the final say.

wrong.Buy, a breakout is a breakout: A 5-minute breakout can time an entry. It can't turn a weekly downtrend into a months-long uptrend.
wrong.Buy, with a tight 5-minute stop: A tight stop limits the loss, but it doesn't fix the plan. You'd be fighting the weekly trend on a 5-minute signal.
wrong.Pass, the 5-minute chart is noise: Right action, wrong reason. A 5-minute chart can time an entry. The reason to pass is the weekly trend, which points down.

questions.simple: Pass, because a hold of months needs the weekly trend on your side, and here it points down.

deeper.trap: A hard 5-minute breakout feels like news the long-term holders missed. But the plan is a months-long hold, so the weekly chart is the one that counts. Under a falling 30-week average, the weekly trend is down. Wait for the weekly picture to change: a close above a 30-week average that is rising again. A close above a still-falling average is not enough.

reasons: Bulkowski on Weinstein plus ChartSchool on Elder and Hill

conflicts: How long each style holds differs by source. Schwab: swing 'days or weeks', position 'weeks or months'. Investopedia's day trader page: swing 'typically days or a few weeks'; its position trading page puts swing traders at 'a few weeks or months'. ChartSchool's Arthur Hill: swing '1-5 day trades', position '1-8 week trades' on end-of-day charts. Bulkowski: Weinstein's method held 2-4 months by a trader. The file keys only the order (day, then swing, then position) and the chart each one leans on, never a fixed range, and quotes Hill only on day traders, commitment and weekly trends, never for his style definitions. W1 says position traders 'many' work off the weekly chart, because Hill's position style uses end-of-day charts.

VWAP on a daily chart: ChartSchool says VWAP 'is not defined for daily, weekly, or monthly periods'; Schwab's VWAP article says 'On a daily chart, the VWAP line alone might be used to identify potential trends'. All three publishers read (ChartSchool, Schwab, Investopedia) agree it is one session's calculation that restarts at the next open, and that is all the file keys (q02, q13). Investopedia's VWAP page also calls 330 minutes 'the length of a typical trading session' (ChartSchool: 390 minutes); that page is not cited.

Pivot periods are StockCharts' convention: 1- to 15-minute charts use the prior day, 30- to 120-minute charts the prior week, daily charts the prior month. Other platforms let the user pick. q15 names the rule as ChartSchool's in the question and keys the calc; q09 uses the standard prior-day pivot for a 5-minute chart.

The unit row (UNITS-foundations.md) names 'ORB, 30-minute pivot, Go Signal for the day'. TRADE_PLANS.md defines the Go Signal as 'an intraday entry' with the stop at the session's low and no exit at the close, so it is not a day trade; F11.03 (written in parallel) asks its stop (q06, whose question gives the 30-minute entry) and its 2R target (q11), so this file leaves it out. (Track audit 2026-11-09: no F11 unit asks the Go Signal's 30 or 65-minute trigger chart as such; it appears only as a given in F11.03 q06.) No house source defines a '30-minute pivot', so it is left out. The opening-range break is taught as an entry that a multi-day plan can use (our Kicker's day-one 30-minute break; ChartSchool's first-hour gap entry, which trails an 8% stop), not as a day-trade-only setup.

Opening range length: ChartSchool's gap strategies wait one hour; our Kicker uses the 30-minute range. q21 says 'opening range' with no length and keys only that a resting buy stop fits a trader who cannot watch.

SEC 'Day Trading: Your Dollars at Risk' was last reviewed 2005-04-20. Its lines on margin and borrowed money are dated: FINRA's intraday margin standards took effect 2026-06-04 (FINRA, Frequent Intraday Trading; Investopedia's day trader page adds a transition to 2027-10-20 for the old pattern day trader test). The file uses only the SEC's timeless lines (holding time, flat overnight, watching continuously, early losses) and quizzes no margin or pattern day trader rule.

Weinstein's rules here are Bulkowski's reading ('Here's my interpretation of his setup'), Tier 2, one publisher. Every key that leans on them also has a second publisher for the principle: q04 (Investopedia and Schwab on position traders, ChartSchool on weekly bars), q11 (a calc), q22 (Elder on ChartSchool: a weekly uptrend before a daily buy; Arthur Hill: long only with weekly bull trends). Bulkowski's own test found stage 2 buys in his trades averaged 4.1%; the file makes no claim about results.

q11: 30 weeks x 5 days = 150 days is a calc over givens. A 30-week average of weekly closes and a 150-day average of daily closes are close but not identical (holidays, and which closes are averaged), so the why says 'sits close to', never 'equals'.

q20: only Investopedia says position trading is 'ideally suited to a bull market with a strong trend' and that day trading 'might have the advantage' in a flat market. The key also rests on Schwab (a position trader holds 'as long as the trend remains intact') and ChartSchool (trend-following signals 'produce many whipsaws' without a strong trend). Swing trading is deliberately not a choice: Schwab says swing traders also trade 'sideways consolidations', so how a swing trader fares in chop is arguable.

Investopedia pages (s17, s18, s19) answer the plain client intermittently (200 for all three on 2026-11-09, including the quote-check run; 403 on other tries) and WebFetch cannot reach investopedia.com. Every key that cites them also stands on another source: q01 (ChartSchool f09), q03 (Bulkowski f52/f53), q04 (Bulkowski, Schwab), q06 (ChartSchool f27), q12 (FINRA f06, Tier 1), q14 (ChartSchool f23/f24), q19 (SEC f01/f02, Tier 1; ChartSchool f08), q20 (Schwab f41, ChartSchool f33).

Overlap with F11.01 and F11.03, written at the same time: this file dropped its drafts that repeated theirs (the daily-setup / hourly-entry pair, the 9-to-5 job picking a style, day trading's time cost, the 3:50 pm day trade exit, the Go Signal's trigger chart, a months-long hold with a tight stop, a 5-minute signal on a long hold). What remains is this unit's own ground: which setups and tools belong to which clock.

Checker, 2026-11-09: anchored VWAP (a separate tool started from a chosen bar) can span days. Every source here describes the session VWAP, which is what q02 and q13 mean by VWAP; anchored VWAP is not taught or keyed.
